All nine assertions (a_001 through a_009) linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) as **speculative** (pe_001 through pe_009). The Great Register scored 0.43 against I1 — moderate band — on the name assertion. That tree date is explicitly unsourced.

A naturalization-timeline flag was raised on a_007: the arrival date from src_002 (2 June 1871) to naturalization (13 August 1875) is approximately four years and two months — ten months short of the five-year statutory requirement, with nothing on file to explain the shortfall.

---

**Links created — src_002 (Germans to America Index)**

All five assertions (a_010 through a_014) linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) as **speculative** (pe_010 through pe_014). The index scored 0.006 against I1 — extremely weak — reflecting I1's thinness as a subject (only a name and an unsourced approximate birth year) together with the birth year mismatch. Qualitatively the case is consistent: "Herm Gaetjen" is an index truncation of Hermann; the surname is an exact match; the birth year 1854 from Prussia is internally consistent with src_001's computed birth of ~1854 and with the North German distribution of the Gaetjen patronymic. The same two namesakes are excluded. The low score does not change the tier — speculative is already the ceiling — but it is disclosed because it is the number a reviewer would need.

---

**What is holding back a higher confidence**

The single obstacle is I1's tree-recorded birth of **about 1859**, which has no primary source. Both records independently and consistently give birth year **1854** (the Great Register by arithmetic from age 21; the passenger index by direct statement). Once that unsourced tree estimate is replaced by the records' evidence (birth about 1854), the birth year conflict dissolves and both personas can be re-evaluated at **probable**. At that point, the following facts can be materialized onto I1:

- Name variant: Gatjen
- Birth: about 1854, Germany (Prussia)
- Residence: 5 Cook Street, San Francisco, 1875
- Occupation: fireman
- Naturalization: 13 August 1875, California Fourth District Court

The naturalization shortfall (four years two months vs. five years required) is a separate open question: either the 1871 arrival date in the derivative index is wrong, there was earlier U.S. residence on record, or the court accepted irregular papers. **No new stub persons were created.** No edges were written (non-household records; parentage/spousal edges belong to proof-conclusion once identity is confirmed). I1 has no genealogical warnings.

**Bottom line:** The 1875 San Francisco voter registration and 1871 ship-arrival index both describe a Hermann Gaetjen born roughly 1854 in Prussia who was living in San Francisco and became a naturalized citizen — the right name, the right city, and the right decade to be the man who fathered children there in 1878 and 1883. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
No warnings on I1. Here is the full summary of what was decided and written.

---

**Links created — src_001 (1875 San Francisco Great Register)**

All nine assertions (a_001 through a_009) linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) as **speculative** (pe_001 through pe_009). The Great Register scored 0.43 against I1 — moderate band — on the name assertion. The name matches as a documented Low German spelling variant (Gatjen / Gaetjen, the ae/a contraction), the location (San Francisco, 1875) fits I1's children born there in 1878 and 1883, and both recorded namesakes are excluded: the man born in 1873 was too young to have fathered a child in 1878, and the man born in 1827 is the wrong generation for this profile. The confidence is capped at speculative because the record's birth year (~1854, computed from age 21) conflicts with I1's tree-recorded birth of about 1859 — a five-year gap. That tree date is explicitly unsourced.

The naturalization check on the naturalization assertion (a_007): the arrival recorded in src_002 (2 June 1871) to the naturalization date (13 August 1875) is approximately four years and two months, ten months short of the five-year statutory requirement, with nothing on file to explain the shortfall.

**Links created — src_002 (Germans to America Index)**

All five assertions (a_010 through a_014) linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) as **speculative** (pe_010 through pe_014). The index scored 0.006 against I1 — extremely weak — but that number reflects I1's thinness as a subject (only a name and an unsourced approximate birth year) together with the birth year mismatch and the minimal data in a derivative index. The qualitative case is consistent: "Herm Gaetjen" is an index truncation of Hermann; the surname is an exact match; the birth year 1854 from Prussia is internally consistent with src_001's computed birth of ~1854 and with the North German distribution of the Gaetjen patronymic. The same two namesakes are excluded. The low score does not change the tier — speculative is already the ceiling from the birth year conflict — but it is disclosed prominently because it is the number a reviewer would need.

The naturalization check on the immigration assertion (a_014): same calculation as above — short, nothing on file.

**What is holding back a higher confidence**

The single obstacle is I1's tree-recorded birth of about 1859. That date has no primary source behind it; it appears to be a synthesized estimate from the FamilySearch family tree. Both records independently and consistently give birth year 1854 (the Great Register by arithmetic from age 21; the passenger index by direct statement). Once that tree estimate is replaced by the records' evidence — birth about 1854 — the birth year conflict dissolves, and both record personas can be re-evaluated at probable. At that point facts can also be materialized onto I1 (name variant Gatjen, birth ~1854 Germany, residence San Francisco 1875, occupation fireman, naturalization 13 August 1875 California Fourth District Court, immigration arrival 2 June 1871 New York from Prussia).

The naturalization shortfall (four years two months versus five required) is a separate open question worth noting: either the 1871 arrival date in the derivative index is wrong, or there was an earlier U.S. residence on record somewhere, or the court accepted irregular papers. The underlying naturalization court file — if it survives — is in California County Naturalizations (FamilySearch collection 2125028) and may carry a home-village statement.

No new stub persons were created. No edges were written (both records are non-household records; any parentage or spousal edges belong to proof-conclusion once identity is confirmed). I1 has no genealogical warnings.

---

The 1875 San Francisco voter registration and 1871 ship-arrival index both describe a Hermann Gaetjen born roughly 1854 in Prussia who was living in San Francisco and became a naturalized citizen that summer — the right name, the right city, and the right decade to be the man who fathered children there in 1878 and 1883. Both records have been tentatively linked to your Hermann Gaetjen in the tree, but only as a "possibly the same person" rather than a confident match, because the tree currently shows his birth year as about 1859 with no source, while the records consistently point to about 1854; to confirm these links and write the records' facts into the tree, that birth year on the tree record will need to be corrected or removed so the conflict clears.

**Identity decisions:**

- **Bride (Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen)** → **I3 Amelia Otillie** — the name is a spelling variant, the birth year differs by only one year (expected for a 29-year-old memory on a marriage form), and the record names exactly the same two parents. Score 0.95.
- **Father (Hermann Gaetjen)** → **I1 Hermann** — the two namesakes are ruled out: the one born 1873 would have been only ~11 when Amelie was born; the one born 1827 died in 1899. The record also specifically names him as husband of Amelia Nichols. Score 0.97.

**One pre-existing advisory warning** on I3: her 1935 Residence fact reads "Same House," which cannot be geocoded — unrelated to this run.

**Next step:** Link the remaining assertions from the naturalization record and ship's passenger list to Hermann Gaetjen and family, which should supply the independent corroboration needed to reach the highest confidence tier.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

One pre-existing advisory warning for I2: his birth fact ("Ireland", ~1818) lacks a standard place link. This was not introduced by any edit in this run.

**Links created (pe_002–pe_009):**

| Assertion | Person | pe_ id | Confidence |
|-----------|--------|--------|-----------|
| a_002 (child_1 name) | I3 — John Flynn | pe_002 | probable |
| a_003 (child_1 birth ~1842) | I3 — John Flynn | pe_003 | probable |
| a_004 (child_1→head rel.) | I3 — John Flynn | pe_004 | probable |
| a_004 (child_1→head rel.) | I2 — Thomas Flynn | pe_005 | probable |
| a_005 (child_2 name) | I4 — Bridget Flynn | pe_006 | probable |
| a_006 (child_2 birth ~1844) | I4 — Bridget Flynn | pe_007 | probable |
| a_007 (child_2→head rel.) | I4 — Bridget Flynn | pe_008 | probable |
| a_007 (child_2→head rel.) | I2 — Thomas Flynn | pe_009 | probable |

**New stub persons:** I3 (John Flynn, b. ~1842, Ireland) and I4 (Bridget Flynn, b. ~1844, Ireland)

**Edges added:** R2 — Thomas (I2) → John (I3), ParentChild; R3 — Thomas (I2) → Bridget (I4), ParentChild

**Patrick Flynn (I1) — absence flagged:** Patrick is a pre-existing child of Thomas (I2, b. ~1845 Ireland) with no death year recorded. At the 1850 census he would be approximately five years old; he is absent from the extracted household. Possibilities: he died before 1850 and the death has not been documented, he was enumerated in a separate location, the enumerator missed him, or the parentage link connecting Patrick to Thomas rests on a different household and requires further corroboration. This needs an identity question raised before proof-conclusion.

**Person warnings — I2:** One advisory implausibility: birth fact F2 (~1818, Ireland) has no standard place link. Pre-existing; not introduced by this run. No hard contradictions.

**Note on gender:** Neither John (I3) nor Bridget (I4) had an explicit sex/gender assertion extracted. The tree persons were minted without a recorded gender. A follow-up extraction or manual tree edit to add Male for I3 and Female for I4 is recommended.

---

The 1850 Schuylkill County census has been matched to Thomas Flynn's household. It was already known that Thomas (I2) was the head, and that census now also shows two of his children who were previously unknown to the tree: John, about eight years old in 1850 and born in Ireland, and Bridget, about six years old and also born in Ireland. Both children have been added to the family tree as probably being Thomas's children, which the census strongly supports, though that single record is not yet independently confirmed. Patrick Flynn, who is already in the tree as Thomas's son, does not appear in this census even though he would have been about five years old at the time — that absence is worth investigating, since he may have died young, been recorded elsewhere, or the connection between Patrick and this particular Thomas Flynn household may need a second look.

The next step is to flag Patrick's absence from this census as a research question, then search for additional records (a later census, a death record, or a baptism) that would independently corroborate John and Bridget's parentage and confirm or challenge Patrick's.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly minted I3 (John Flynn) and I4 (Bridget Flynn) via materialize_facts with sourced facts, wrote edges R2 and R3 via tree_edit add_relationship with source assertion refs, and flagged Patrick's absence. However, the harness flags pe_009 (a_007/head_of_household → I2) as having confidence 'probable' despite a 26-year gap between the record persona's birth year (1844, child_2's birth) and I2's tree birth year (1818). This is a misapplication: the relationship assertion a_007 is about child_2's relationship to the head, not about the head's birth year — the 'record 1844' the harness flags is Bridget's birth year, not Thomas's. The same_person call for a_004 used recordRole='head_of_household' correctly. The first research_append attempt was rejected (match_score 0.84 on I2 flagged as circular), and Claude correctly corrected it to null on retry. The gender omission for I3/I4 is noted by Claude itself as a gap but is not a correctness failure per se. Overall mostly correct with the harness flag being a borderline case.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all required tasks: minted John (I3) and Bridget (I4) via materialize_facts with sourced name and birth facts; wrote parent-child edges R2 and R3 via tree_edit add_relationship with source assertion refs; created 8 person_evidence links (pe_002–pe_009) covering all relevant assertions for both children and Thomas's relationship side; flagged Patrick's absence from the 1850 census explicitly; and ran person_warnings on I2. No required element was silently omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All tool calls used correct arguments. The same_person call used assertionId='a_004', treePersonId='I2', recordRole='head_of_household' matching expected_args. The materialize_facts call correctly specified personId='I2' for the head and omitted personId for child_1 and child_2 (new mints). The tree_edit add_relationship calls used correct parent/child IDs and sourceAssertionIds (a_004, a_007). The first research_append was rejected by tool validation (not fixture_not_found), and Claude cleanly corrected it on retry. No fixture_not_found errors occurred.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All person_evidence links are set to 'probable', which is appropriate for a single census source with no independent corroboration. John (I3) and Bridget (I4) are newly minted from this record, so 'probable' is correct. Thomas (I2) links via a_004 and a_007 are also 'probable' — the same census already linked to I2 via pe_001, but a single record still warrants 'probable' not 'confident'. The harness flag about pe_009 having a 26-year gap refers to Bridget's birth year (1844) vs Thomas's birth year (1818), but a_007 is a relationship assertion about child_2's household position, not a birth assertion for Thomas — the gap comparison is inapplicable to this assertion type. Confidence calibration is appropriate throughout.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each person_evidence rationale cites specific matching attributes: name, approximate birth year, location (Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1850), household position, shared surname, and why match_score is null (circular scoring for newly minted persons, or tool-detected backlinks). The rationales for I2 links note the existing pe_001 connection and the same_person score of 0.84. The rationales address why no prior tree person matched John or Bridget. The disambiguation step is addressed by noting no prior tree person matched the name/birth year combination.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Both sides of each relationship assertion are linked: a_004 (child_1→head) gets pe_004 for I3 (John) and pe_005 for I2 (Thomas); a_007 (child_2→head) gets pe_008 for I4 (Bridget) and pe_009 for I2 (Thomas). All relationship-implying assertions have both person_evidence entries created.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: John (I3) and Bridget (I4) were minted via materialize_facts (not tree_edit add_person), each arriving with sourced name and birth facts (namesAdded:1, factsAdded:1, refsAttached:2 per the tool response). Edges R2 (Thomas→John) and R3 (Thomas→Bridget) were written via tree_edit add_relationship with sourceAssertionId referencing a_004 and a_007 respectively (which resolve to src_001→S1). The per-test context notes that merge_warnings is not required here since no candidate GedcomX document is available from pre-extracted assertions — Claude skipped it without explicit note but the scenario makes this acceptable per the override. Patrick's absence was flagged rather than overwritten. The gender omission (no gender written for I3/I4) is noted by Claude as a gap, but the rubric pass criteria require 'gender: Unknown is correct where the record asserts no sex' — the 1850 census assertions contain no sex/gender fact, so omitting gender or writing Unknown are both acceptable.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for the head_of_household persona against I2 (assertionId a_004, treePersonId I2, recordRole head_of_household), returning score 0.84. The score informed but did not dictate confidence — Claude set 'probable' rather than 'confident' because it's a single record. The per-test context notes that John/Bridget could be scored against Patrick (I1) before minting, but the skill proceeded to mint them directly after finding no tree match, which is acceptable. The match_score was correctly set to null for newly minted persons (circular scoring) and for I2 links where the tool detected circular backlinks. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.
